turns.text: What do you remember about the moment you found out you’d be sent down from Shanghai to the countryside?

I was sitting at the kitchen table, peeling potatoes for dinner, when my father came in with a slip of paper in his hand. He didn’t say much—just put it down and told me to read. The words were stiff and official, but I understood right away: I was to leave for the Northeast, to the Beidahuang. My mother made a sound behind me, sharp and quick, but then she swallowed it and started moving around the kitchen, louder than before, as if noise could keep the news from settling in. I remember the smell of raw potato on my hands, and the way the light outside looked—gray, like it was already winter. My youngest sister clung to my arm and asked if I’d bring her candy when I came back. I didn’t know what to say, because I didn’t know if I’d come back at all.

I can almost feel how heavy that moment was, especially with your mother trying to fill the silence and your sister not understanding what it really meant. When you were finally alone that evening, what did you do, and what thoughts ran through your mind as you tried to fall asleep?

That night, I lay on my narrow bed and stared at the ceiling, tracing the cracks in the plaster with my eyes. I could hear my parents’ voices through the thin wall—low, sometimes breaking off, sometimes rising, then quiet again. I tried to imagine what the Northeast would look like. In my head, it was just a white blur, endless snow, and wind that never stopped. I thought about the friends I’d leave behind, the city streets I knew by heart, the little bakery at the corner where I used to buy steamed buns. I wondered if I’d have to eat potatoes every day, if I’d be cold all the time, if I would ever see Shanghai again. I pressed my hands together under the blanket, trying to hold onto the warmth, and I didn’t sleep much at all.

The first night after I got the notice, sleep felt impossible. I kept listening to the sounds of the house—my father’s cough, the creak of floorboards, my mother’s footsteps going back and forth. I remember the taste of fear in my mouth, metallic and sour. I thought about what would happen to my sisters after I left—who would help with the chores, who would keep them out of trouble at school, who would be there when my mother’s temper flared. I kept replaying my last walk through the alley near our apartment, the smell of coal smoke and fried dough, the neighbor’s radio playing some old revolutionary song. I tried to picture myself in the countryside but couldn’t see anything except a blank, cold space. I felt like I was already halfway gone, even though I was still in my own bed.

Your memories of home—the sounds, the smells, the worries about your sisters—make it clear how much you were leaving behind before you even stepped out the door. You mentioned the neighbor’s radio playing a revolutionary song; do you remember how you felt about those songs and slogans at that point, hearing them from your own apartment?

By then, those songs felt like wallpaper—always there, impossible to ignore, but stripped of meaning. When I was younger, I used to sing along with my classmates, waving little red flags, believing it was all for something bright and important. But that night, the music grated on me. It seemed to mock the heaviness in our home. I remember wishing I could turn it off, just for an hour, so I could hear my own thoughts. The slogans, too, were everywhere—painted on walls, shouted at school, printed on handouts. They used to make me feel part of something, but now they just reminded me how little control I had over my own future.

There was a time when I thought those songs meant hope, or at least a kind of belonging. But that night, I felt only resentment. The melody drifted through the walls, bright and relentless, as if it was meant to drown out any private sorrow. I remember how the words—about loyalty and sacrifice—felt hollow, almost cruel, when I was facing the reality of being sent away. The slogans on the walls outside our building had started to fade and peel, but they still glared at me every time I walked past. I felt like they were watching, making sure I didn’t forget who was really making the decisions. I wanted to cover my ears, but even silence couldn’t keep the slogans out. They were in the air, in the way people looked at each other, in the way my parents avoided saying certain things. That night, I realized those words had nothing to do with me anymore.

It’s striking how the slogans became almost like another set of eyes, always present and impossible to escape, even in silence. You mentioned your parents avoiding certain topics—can you remember something they left unsaid that night, and how that silence shaped your own feelings as you prepared to leave?

What they didn’t say was almost louder than what they did. My father never asked if I was scared, and my mother didn’t talk about what I should do if things went badly. Nobody said anything about missing each other, or about how long it might be before I could come home. Instead, they stuck to practical things—what clothes to pack, how to keep warm, which foods would last on the journey. The silence around everything else made me feel both more alone and more responsible, like I had to carry all the fear and sadness by myself. It was as if saying the truth out loud would make it even more real, so we all pretended not to see it. That silence stayed with me, even after I left.

I remember sitting at the table with my mother, folding my clothes into a bundle, her hands moving quickly but her face turned away. She told me to wear layers, to keep my money hidden, to watch out for lice. My father just stood in the doorway, arms crossed, staring at the floor. He didn’t say anything about what might happen if I got sick, or if I wanted to come home—he just said to listen, to work hard, to not draw attention. I waited for him to say something about being proud, or about hoping I’d be safe, but he never did. The air felt thick with things we couldn’t say. I kept wishing someone would tell me what to do if I couldn’t bear it, but all I got were instructions on how to sew up a torn coat. That silence made me feel like I was already gone, like I was leaving a hole behind that nobody wanted to look at.

The way your parents focused on practical advice, but avoided any talk of fear or longing, makes me think about how families tried to protect each other by not naming their pain. When you were finally on the train heading north, did you find yourself replaying any of those unsaid words—or did the journey itself push all that aside?

On the train, I sat by the window with my bundle on my lap, watching the city slip away and the landscape change from gray buildings to flat, empty fields. At first, I kept thinking about all the things we didn’t say—my mother’s face when she turned away, my father’s silence, the way my sisters clung to me at the station but didn’t cry. I replayed those moments over and over, searching for some hidden meaning or message in the way my father handed me a hard-boiled egg, or how my mother tucked a pair of wool socks into my bag at the last minute. But after a while, the motion of the train and the unfamiliar faces around me took over. The rhythm of the wheels on the tracks, the smell of steamed buns and coal smoke in the carriage, the cold that seeped in through the windows—it all became louder than the silence I carried from home. By the second day, I was too tired and hungry to think about what had been left unsaid. Survival pushed everything else aside.

On that train, the ache of what wasn’t spoken followed me like a shadow at first. I pressed my forehead to the glass, searching the passing scenery for something familiar, but there was nothing—just the tracks stretching into nowhere. I kept fingering the little things my mother had packed, as if I could squeeze comfort out of them. The egg, the socks, a tiny cloth pouch with a few coins sewn inside. Each item felt like a secret apology for all the words she hadn’t said. But as the hours dragged on, the air in the carriage grew thick with other people’s uncertainty and fear. There were whispered conversations about what might happen, and a few tried to hum those old songs, but mostly we sat in silence, wrapped in our own worries. Hunger made my hands shake, and I rationed my food, counting out bites. By the time the train lurched to a stop in the cold north, I had stopped listening for the voices of home. All I could hear was the wind, sharper and emptier than anything I’d known before.

The way you describe the little objects from home—especially the pouch with coins sewn inside—makes me realize how much meaning you found in those small gestures. When you first stepped off the train into that northern wind, what was the very first thing you noticed, and how did that moment change your sense of what lay ahead?
